newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland debates financing flood relief action.
newsitem.headline: Poland debates financing flood relief action.

text.p: Debate in Poland on how to finance the reconstruction of areas hit by July's catastrophic flooding gained new momentum on Friday as the prime minister criticised opposition proposals to issue special flood bonds.

Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said the government had enough funds for now to proceed with relief operations so it did not need the bonds, which would destabilise the financial market if offered at high yields or on a tax-deductible basis.

"If we encourage people to buy bonds with high interest and tax deductions we should know that this would only... increase public spending, which would in the long term cripple the budget's ability to remove the flood damages," the premier said during a special parliamentary debate on the flood.

Meanwhile the flood waters receded further despite showers in many parts of the country, but a struggle continued along the Oder River on the German border to save sodden dikes, in danger of breaking and causing new flooding.

Cimoszewicz said early this week that the government would consider the tax-deductible bond proposal by the opposition Solidarity Election Action (AWS), his ex-communist party main rival in general elections on September 21.

But on Thursday Finance Minister Marek Belka unveiled plans to introduce a special temporary flood tax next year to raise up to two billion zlotys for the reconstruction in the least inflationary way, a proposal the AWS instantly criticised.
"The tax is the least creative solution. Our bond proposal is a non-inflationary measure...which will stimulate the capital market," AWS spokesman Tomasz Tywonek said.
The government will make a final decision on whether to impose the tax or issue the flood bonds during its debate on the 1998 budget draft, due in late August and early September.

Cimoszewicz said the government now had nearly 500 million zlotys ($144 million) squeezed from this year's budget and $200 million in the credit line from the World Bank, which was enough for flood relief for the time being.
The government would seek a further $300 million in loans from the World Bank and other financial institutions, he said.
The EU, whose Commissioner for Humanitarian Aid Emma Bonino visited Poland on Friday, has allowed Warsaw to use some 260 million zlotys from its PHARE aid scheme for the flood relief.
Bonino assured Poles her humanitarian aid office, which has decided to provide seven million zlotys for Poland, was ready to increase the assistance should the need arise.
But despite aid and loans, the finance minister has already said the flood would be the focus of the next budget so other areas could expect very modest spending.
The AWS, comprised of groups that overthrew communism in 1989, has said it will change the inherited budget draft if it wins in the polls but vowed to pursue tight financial policies.
The ex-communists, in power since 1993 along with a peasant party, and the AWS are running neck-in-neck in opinion polls.

Many analysts fear the flood, which hit southwestern Poland four weeks ago causing damage amounting to billions of dollars, will aggravate the country's trouble with trade and current account gaps and plunge its economy into recession.

On Friday, the central bank announced its interest rates rise to curb booming domestic demand, which is fuelling the current account deficit and posing a threat to the government's plan to cut inflation to 13 percent in December from 15.4 percent in June.
The bank said it would increase its discount rate by 2.5 points to 24.5 percent and the lombard rate by two points to 27 percent, effective from Monday.
The increase is partly meant to offset effect of the 2.5 percent loan, which parliament allowed the government to draw from the central bank this year as an extraordinary measure.
($ = 3.472 Polish Zlotys)
